IFF's Statement on web censorship accompanying the elections results in Tamil Nadu and swearing in of C. Joseph Vijay

Recent reports around C. Joseph Vijay’s swearing in as Tamil Nadu Chief Minister point to a familiar problem in India’s web censorship architecture where political speech is being restricted through a mix of formal takedown notices, opaque platform enforcement, and disputed claims of government involvement. Here, the regulatory framework for this has been created by the Union Government acting through the Ministry of Electronics and IT which has continued to amend and expand censorship powers under the IT Rules, 2021.

On May 8, 2026, a notice was issued by the Tamil Nadu Police Cyber Crime Wing to X Corp, directing the removal or blocking of 18 URLs within three hours. The earliest accessible press report we found is PTI’s copy carried by The Print on May 10 at 8:49 PM IST, which states that the notice invoked Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the IT Rules, 2021, and described the posts as “unlawful”, “provocative” and capable of disturbing public order.

This sits alongside two related platform incidents. First, Rahul Gandhi’s Instagram reel and photo post featuring Vijay’s swearing in were reportedly blocked or restricted after going viral. The earliest publicly accessible report alleging such restriction appears to be Congress leader Srivatsa’s X post of May 10, which was embedded or quoted by The Week, PTI/Daily Pioneer, ANI, and IANS. These reports also record MeitY’s denial, with government sources attributing the restriction to Instagram’s internal systems mistakenly flagging the post. While the post was later restored, the brief restriction impeded its reach and virality. Second, the official X handle of the Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK) was reportedly suspended shortly after a purported post supporting TVK’s coalition bid. X permanently or temporarily suspended the official VCK handle, displaying the standard notice that the account “violated X rules.” No further public explanation was provided by X.

Taken together, these incidents show how web censorship now operates through a blurred chain of responsibility. Sometimes a public authority or state government acts directly, as with the Tamil Nadu Police notice to X. Sometimes platforms restrict content while users are left with vague references to “legal requirements” or the IT Rules. The result is the same that political speech is interrupted at moments of democratic significance, while the public is left without clear information on who ordered the restriction, under what law, and with what remedy. Such abrupt and arbitrary restrictions also interfere with uncovering an accurate timeline or record of historical events, like assembly elections.

IFF emphasises that legality and process cannot be afterthoughts. Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021 requires “actual knowledge” through a court order or notification by the appropriate government or its agency under Section 79(3)(b). In Shreya Singhal, the Supreme Court read Section 79(3)(b) narrowly and held that such court orders or government notifications must conform to Article 19(2). IFF calls on all public authorities and platforms to disclose the legal notices, affected URLs, issuing authorities, timelines of restriction and restoration, and remedies available to affected users. 

We also call on social media companies to do better since automating content moderation on the basis of laws and rules cannot become a shield for arbitrary restriction and the IT Rules, 2021 cannot be allowed to function as a shadow censorship system in which political speech disappears first and explanations arrive later, if at all.

Internet Freedom Foundation
May 11, 2026
Delhi

Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79

5 November 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is alarmed by the Indian Express that the Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes. 

This is also the latest step in an escalation that has been building for years. The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour. 

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance. 

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.
Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

What IFF will do

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content. The public has a right to know who is in the room when the rules of their speech are being rewritten.

We will publish what we receive, and we invite other civil society groups, journalists and platform users to join us in asking the Ministry to put any proposal to open consultation before it goes anywhere near Parliament.

text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Bad becomes worse? Further changes proposed to the proposed changes to IT Rules!

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

India's government blocked 129 betting websites this year on the strength of 2 court orders that turned out to be fake, a Reuters investigation found.

The Department of Telecommunications sent blocking orders to internet companies on 21 July and 2 September. Each came with a "court order" that claimed to be from the Allahabad High Court or the Rajasthan High Court.

Neither order shows up in the courts' own records. After Reuters asked about it, the Allahabad High Court said its order was fake and filed a police complaint on 6 November. Police have opened a case of forgery and cheating against unknown people.

Reuters could not find out who made the fake orders, or whether AI was used to make them. The telecom department did not reply to Reuters' questions.

India's system for taking content off the internet is one of the strictest in the world. This case shows fake papers can still get through it.

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

The app uses iOS's VPN framework but is NOT a real VPN. It doesn't hide your IP or change location. It just reroutes DNS queries system-wide. Free, no signup, made by Cloudflare.

2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on
5. Preferred: 1.1.1.1 | Alternate: 1.0.0.1
6. Save

Press Windows key → type "cmd" → right-click "Command Prompt" → Run as administrator → Yes. Black window opens. Type ipconfig /flushdns, press Enter.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Delhi ahead of the 10 October protest. The order remains unpublished, and the police communication conveying it is marked "Top Secret".

9 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the internet shutdown imposed in parts of Delhi ahead of the protest called for tomorrow, 10 October 2026, at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. A communication dated 9 October 2026 from the Deputy Commissioner of Police, Special Cell (HQ), Delhi to the nodal officers of Airtel, Vodafone Idea, Jio and MTNL, shared by the news agency ANI, records that the Union Home Secretary has authorised, on the request of the Delhi Police, the suspension of "mobile internet services (all technologies)" within a radius of four kilometres of the Janpath-Kartavya Path crossing, from 10 pm on 9 October to 10 pm on 10 October 2026. It refers to order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and is marked "Top Secret" at the top and bottom of the page.

As per a media report by Live Law, the Solicitor General informed the Supreme Court today that the shutdown is confined to "certain sensitive pockets" and will be reviewed on the basis of security inputs. The communication describes a circle of about 50 square kilometres across the centre of the capital, which takes in Jantar Mantar, Connaught Place, India Gate, Parliament, the Supreme Court, the Delhi High Court, New Delhi Railway Station and hospitals including Ram Manohar Lohia and Lady Hardinge. This is about seven times the area of the suspension ordered around Jantar Mantar on 2 October, and it runs for twice as long.

Delhi Police has refused permission for the protest, and prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force in New Delhi district. Delhi Police asked for the gates of 57 metro stations to be closed from 9 pm today, and the Railways cancelled trains due at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin between 4 am and 2 pm tomorrow. Hearing a challenge to these measures today, the Supreme Court directed that there be no complete prohibition on metro and train services and asked the authorities to keep in mind the principle of proportionality. As reported, that order did not examine the internet shutdown. We call for the order to be withdrawn, and for mobile internet to remain available across Delhi tomorrow.

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public knows the area and hours of this shutdown from a police communication marked "Top Secret" that was shared by ANI, and not from the government. That communication records no reasons, and the order of the Union Home Secretary to which it refers has not been made public. This is now a pattern and the order for the shutdown of 2 October around Jantar Mantar became public four days later, when the Hindu obtained a copy.

This secrecy is contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Court held that "an order, particularly one that affects lives, liberty and property of people, must be made available". It directed the authorities to "publish all orders in force and any future orders" suspending telecom services, including the internet, "to enable the affected persons to challenge it before the High Court or appropriate forum". A democracy "sworn to transparency and accountability", the Court said, "necessarily mandates the production of orders as it is the right of an individual to know". The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, framed under Section 20 of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, now provide that every suspension order "shall be published", must state its reasons, and must be limited to a clearly defined geographical area and a specified duration. No order may be made unless the authority has considered that its objectives cannot be achieved by any other reasonable means.

The communication shared by ANI invokes Rule 3 of these Rules, the same Rule that requires the order to be published. It is nevertheless marked "Top Secret", the highest security classification used by the Government of India. In January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs issued orders bearing the same number to suspend the internet at Singhu, Ghazipur and Tikri during the farmers' protest, and those orders remain available on the Ministry's own website. An order cannot be published and kept "Top Secret" at the same time.

The government has placed no evidence before the public that a shutdown makes a protest safer. The available research is to the contrary as a 2019 study of shutdowns and protest in India by Jan Rydzak, then at Stanford's Global Digital Policy Incubator, found shutdowns "much more strongly associated with increases in violent collective action than with non-violent mobilization". The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights reported in 2022 that many shutdowns justified on grounds of public safety or national security "were followed by spikes in violence" (A/HRC/50/55). In December 2021, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology recorded that neither the Department of Telecommunications nor the Ministry of Home Affairs had studied the impact of shutdowns.

A shutdown also prevents people from documenting and reporting what happens at a protest. The same UN report found that, “the inability to access tools to document and rapidly report abuses seems to contribute to further violence”. Without mobile internet, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A protester cannot upload a video as events unfold, and a person who is injured or detained cannot send a location to family or a lawyer. On 20 July 2026, mobile internet in Central Delhi was switched off amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters. In Manipur in 2023, video of an assault on two women on 4 May reached the public only on 19 July, while a shutdown imposed on 3 May was still in force. This is the impact an internet shutdown has which rather than preventing violence prevents the documentation of illegality.

Our demands:

We call upon the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Delhi Police to:
1) Withdraw order No. 22016/12/2019-CIS-IV dated 9 October 2026 and keep mobile internet services running across Delhi on 10 October 2026.
2) Publish that order, and every other suspension order issued in connection with the protest, forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.
3) Withdraw the "Top Secret" marking, and stop classifying suspension orders and the communications that convey them to telecom operators.
4) Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and publish its final order, as the Supreme Court required on 23 February 2024.
5) Ensure that journalists and members of the public can record and report from the protest sites without obstruction.

text:
The Prime Minister's Office called in India's telecom secretary, Amit Agrawal, on Saturday, after it came out that the government blocked websites using 2 fake court orders. He cut short a trip to another state for the meeting.

Reuters reported this week that the telecom department told internet companies to block as many as 129 illegal betting websites this year, based on orders that looked like they came from the Allahabad and Rajasthan High Courts. Both courts say the orders are fake.

The papers had court seals and a QR code, so they looked real. They stayed on the telecom department's own website for months. As of Saturday, only one of the 2 had been taken down.

Police have opened a case for forgery and cheating. No one has been arrested yet.

The worry is about how website blocking works in India. If a fake order can get sites blocked, the same trick could be used to take down websites that did nothing wrong.

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
GOOGLE YIELDS TO SEOUL: SOUTH KOREAN COORDINATES STRIPPED FROM MAPS AND EARTH

South Korea forced Google to erase latitude and longitude coordinates for its territory from Google Maps and Google Earth. The move meets a hard security condition attached to a February 2026 export permit for high-precision map data that Seoul had blocked for nearly two decades.

Officials confirmed the removal after reviewing Google’s compliance report. The same conditions require deletion of Street View imagery inside and around military and security facilities. The government warned it will suspend or revoke the permit for serious breaches.

Seoul rejected identical requests in 2007 and 2016, citing the risk that detailed maps could expose sensitive military sites. The February approval ended that standoff only after Google accepted the restrictions, including reliance on a domestic partner, TMAP Mobility, to process security-screened imagery and base data.

Standard GPS navigation and everyday map functions remain available. The change targets the public display and export of precise coordinates that could be exploited, not the underlying positioning systems used by phones and vehicles. Google built a dedicated control layer for Korean territory and a safeguard to block app updates that re-expose the data.

This is a clear assertion of national security priorities over unrestricted corporate data access. After years of resistance, South Korea secured the protections it demanded before allowing its detailed geospatial information onto foreign servers.

Appeal Number: MINIT/E/A/26/0001675

When a citizen exhausts every available grievance redressal mechanism, who holds the system accountable?

For five months, I have been struggling with unresolved issues concerning Facebook and its grievance redressal process in India.

I filed five grievances through the Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC). Two were rejected as premature without clear justification, while two were disposed of without meaningful resolution.

I subsequently approached the Prime Minister's Office through CPGRAMS, explicitly requesting direct intervention and asking that my grievance not be routed through the same officials who had previously handled my complaints without providing meaningful relief.

What happened?

My grievance was once again assigned to the same officer who had disposed of my earlier regular CPGRAMS complaint.

On 11 November 2026, my grievance was closed with a generic response explaining the IT Rules, 2021 and advising me to approach Facebook's Grievance Officer.

But my actual concerns remain unanswered.

Was Facebook's allegedly incorrect information submitted to GAC examined?

Were my previous complaints and supporting evidence reviewed?

Why was my explicit request for independent, higher-level intervention not addressed?

I have now formally escalated the matter to the Nodal Officer through CPGRAMS.

I am not seeking preferential treatment. I am seeking transparency, accountability and an impartial examination of my grievance.

A grievance redressal mechanism must deliver more than registration numbers and disposal remarks. It must deliver meaningful justice.

I respectfully request the intervention of the concerned authorities and an independent review by an appropriate senior authority.

If a citizen follows every prescribed procedure and still cannot obtain a meaningful response, where is that citizen supposed to go next?

@PMOIndia @GoI_MeitY @SecretaryMEITY @DARPGSEVA

#DigitalIndia #CitizenRights #Accountability #GrievanceRedressal

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

If your post or account was withheld or removed in connection with the protests, or you received a notice about a police data request, write to legal@internetfreedom.in for pro bono assistance. Keep screenshots of every notice, note the date and time, and delete nothing. Document, document, document.

If you got hit by this Trusted Chat AI banwave, here is the actual methodology. Don't just spam appeals, you'll get blacklisted. Here is how to fight it:

First, look at your ban screen. If it says "Decision method: We used automated systems" and "More details aren't available," screenshot it. That proves a bot banned you with zero evidence and no human review.

Second, the standard support form is useless right now. Email privacy@roblox.com with the subject "GDPR Article 15 Data Access Request." Tell them you want all your chat logs and moderation records. If the bot replies telling you to use the self-serve portal, reply back and say "I cannot use self-serve because my account is banned. Please assist me via this ticket." That forces their legal team to open a real ticket for you.

Third, if they claim they can't verify your email or you get a weird login error, check your Google Play or Apple receipts. Send them the order number. Billing proof is undeniable and proves you own the account.

Fourth, if you want to try the fast unban that worked for some people, submit a ticket saying you apologize for the misunderstanding, you understand the automated system is sensitive even in Trusted DMs, and you'll be more careful. It sucks to apologize for a bot's mistake, but it works for some.

Fifth, if you're in the EU, use your rights. File a free dispute with ADR Center under Article 21 of the DSA. File with Verbraucherzentrale if you're in Germany. And email jugendschutzbeauftragter-roblox@usk.de because if they are falsely flagging adults for child safety, the German youth protection team needs to know.

An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
The Tribune 19 July 2026

text:
🔍 Does an Adjournment Order Extending the Existing Interim Protection Decide the GST Dispute on Merits?
⚖️ The Verdict: The Gauhati High Court granted the Petitioner three weeks to file a rejoinder affidavit and directed that the existing interim order would continue until the next hearing.

📌 The Dispute
• N.C. Das and Company had filed a writ petition against the Union of India and GST authorities before the Gauhati High Court.
• On 10.11.2026, the Court granted three weeks to the Petitioner to file a rejoinder to the Respondents' affidavit-in-opposition and directed the matter to be listed thereafter.

📚 The Legal Basis

Statement: Proposed withdrawal of safe harbour under Section 79

5 November 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation is alarmed by the Indian Express that the Ministry of Electronics and IT has begun discussions on stripping social media platforms of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000. Nobody should mistake this for a move against Big Tech for it is a move against the people who use these platforms.

Safe harbour is not a gift to Meta, Google or X. It is the legal foundation that lets ordinary Indians speak online without a platform's lawyers deciding in advance whether their post is worth the risk and taking it down. If it is taken away, and every platform becomes liable for every post, comment and video. The rational response for any company is to remove anything that might draw a complaint, a notice or a summons. Criticism of the government, reporting on protests, satire, and the speech of people without lawyers will be the first casualties which are already being censored by automated filters implemented pursuant to the IT Rules, 2021. The Supreme Court recognised exactly this in Shreya Singhal (2015), which is why it read down Section 79(3)(b) to require a court order or a lawful government direction before platforms must act.

The timing tells its own story as the report says that MEITY’s rethink was shaped by a view within government that platform algorithms have favoured Opposition and anti-establishment narratives over official messaging, and by the role of Instagram during the student protests in July. In other words, the complaint is not that platforms host too much illegal content but it is that they host too much content the government dislikes. 

This is also the latest step in an escalation that has been building for years. The 2023 Fact Check Unit amendment tried to make the government the arbiter of truth about itself, until the Bombay High Court struck it down. The Sahyog portal has turned Section 79(3)(b) into a parallel, opaque takedown channel that sidesteps the safeguards of Section 69A, a practice X is now challenging in court. In August, a Parliamentary Standing Committee gave Mark Zuckerberg three days to apologise personally for the brief removal of the Prime Minister's video or face the loss of safe harbour. 

Subsequently advisories were issued on October 8, 2026 and October 10, 2026 pressuring digital platforms to implement pro-active censorship through, “enhanced due diligence”. Safe harbour was never meant to be a bargaining chip that MEITY waves at a company to extract compliance. 

There are real problems on these platforms such as child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery and deepfakes. The Supreme Court's observations in Just Rights for Children Alliance on October 15 deserve a serious answer. But the answer is targeted, rights-respecting obligations with independent oversight, transparency about takedowns, and a grievance process that works for users. It is not a liability regime that pushes platforms to delete first and never ask. Nor is it a rule that platforms must clear product changes with the government before shipping them, which would hand the state a license raj over the design of the services Indians use every day.
Any change of this scale must go through Parliament, with a published draft, a genuine consultation and a full debate. It cannot be settled in closed-door meetings between the Ministry and a handful of companies.

What IFF will do

IFF will send a detailed representation to the Ministry of Electronics and IT setting out why the proposed changes to Section 79 are unconstitutional and unworkable, and what a rights-respecting approach to platform accountability should look like. We will also write to the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology.

We are filing RTI applications with MeitY seeking the minutes, agendas, attendance lists and file notings of every meeting held on the review of safe harbour, including the meetings with Meta and other platforms in July and August, and the basis for the Ministry's assessment of how platform algorithms treat government and Opposition content. The public has a right to know who is in the room when the rules of their speech are being rewritten.

We will publish what we receive, and we invite other civil society groups, journalists and platform users to join us in asking the Ministry to put any proposal to open consultation before it goes anywhere near Parliament.

Privacy vs Press Freedom: Where Should the Line Be Drawn? https://t.co/lMP2vkkXLu

🔸The Challenge to the DPDP Act
- Petitioner
DNPA (21 publishers); petition filed 6 October, stay sought 27 October.

- Concerns
Could expose sources, force removal of reports and deter whistleblowers.

- Consent problem
Seeking consent from subjects = 'pre-censorship' (Madhavi Divan).

- No exemption
The Act has no specific journalistic exemption.

🔸Relevant Provisions of the DPDP Act
- Section 3(c)(ii)
Excludes data made public by the person or under a legal duty – a limited exclusion.

- Sections 4–6
Grounds, notice and consent for processing personal data.

- Section 8
Duties of data fiduciaries – security, accuracy, erasure.

- Section 17
Exemptions for legal proceedings, law enforcement, research – not journalism.

🔸The Constitutional Balance
- Right to Privacy
Article 21 – dignity, autonomy, personal data (K.S. Puttaswamy, 2017).

- Press freedom
Article 19(1)(a) – investigate and report on public interest.

- Limits
Both are not absolute; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.

🔸Key Judgments
- R. Rajagopal (1994)
'Auto Shankar case' – officials can't use privacy to block reports on official conduct; no prior restraint.

- R.K. Anand (2009)
Upheld a sting operation exposing an attempt to subvert the BMW trial.

- Manu Sharma (2010)
Warned against media trials that turn suspects into convicts.

- Sahara v. SEBI (2012)
Courts may postpone reporting if there is real risk to a fair trial.

- Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014)
Sting journalism gives no blanket immunity for unlawful acts.

- Axel Springer v. Germany (2012)
ECHR Grand Chamber (12–5) upheld a newspaper's report on an actor's arrest as public-interest journalism.

🔸Global Approaches
- USA
First Amendment; Privacy Protection Act, 1980 limits searches of journalists' work.

- UK
Data Protection Act, 2018 – exemption if publication is in the public interest.

- Brazil
General Data Protection Law excludes journalisticprocessing.

- Kenya
Section 52, Data Protection Act, 2019 – conditional exemption.

- International law
Articles 17 & 19 ICCPR; Articles 8 & 10 ECHR.

🔸Way Forward
- Journalistic exemption
A narrow, public-interest exemption in the DPDP framework.

- Public interest test
Separate genuine scrutiny from needless intrusion.

- Source protection
Protect sources while ensuring accuracy and fairness.

- Proportionality
Restrictions must be necessary and proportionate.

Introduction

🌟 The article highlights the tension between electoral-roll purification and citizens' democratic rights, arguing that the Election Commission must restore public trust through transparency, accountability and procedural fairness.

Main Facts

🌟 ECI foundation: The Election Commission of India was established on January 25, 1950; National Voters' Day has been observed since 2011.

🌟 SIR controversy: The Special Intensive Revision has triggered concerns over mass voter deletions and procedural irregularities.

🌟 Scale of deletion: The ECI reportedly cited approximately 2.8 crore deceased entries removed during the exercise.

Challenges

🌟 Inaccurate electoral databases and mapping discrepancies.

🌟 Procedural barriers affecting legitimate voters.

🌟 Administrative delays in appellate tribunals.

🌟 Declining institutional credibility and public confidence.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Electoral accuracy cannot justify arbitrary disenfranchisement.

🌟 Technological efficiency must complement human verification.

🌟 Institutional neutrality requires transparent decision-making.

🌟 Accountability must accompany the constitutional authority of the ECI.

Way Forward

🌟 Ensure transparent, verifiable electoral-roll revisions.

🌟 Provide accessible notice, hearings and appeals.

🌟 Establish time-bound grievance-redress mechanisms.

🌟 Strengthen independent audits and judicial oversight.

🌟 Prioritise voter restoration and institutional accountability.

🌟 Electoral democracy derives legitimacy not merely from conducting elections, but from ensuring that every eligible citizen retains an effective and dignified right to vote.

The Centre has issued a notice to messaging platform Telegram, directing it to take concrete measures within 15 days to curb the widespread circulation of pirated films, OTT content and other copyrighted audio-visual material on its platform.

The notice, issued by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting (I&B) on July 4, asks Telegram to strengthen its mechanisms for detecting, reporting, disabling access to and removing infringing content. The move is aimed at safeguarding India's creator economy, film industry, broadcasters, OTT platforms, producers and distributors.

The government has also instructed the platform to take action against repeat offenders, including channels, groups, bots, accounts, administrators and associated entities involved in the dissemination of pirated content.

In addition, Telegram has been asked to furnish details of its grievance redressal mechanism available to producers, OTT platforms and law-enforcement agencies, and to submit an Action Taken Report within 15 days outlining the measures implemented to prevent and remove piracy-related material.

The notice signals a shift towards greater platform accountability rather than relying solely on individual takedown requests. The government has previously acted against more than 3,000 Telegram channels allegedly carrying pirated content.

The development comes amid increasing scrutiny of digital platforms over content regulation and compliance. Telegram was also temporarily blocked in India until June 22 in connection with concerns surrounding the NEET-UG re-examination process following allegations of a paper leak and a subsequent investigation by the Central Bureau of Investigation.

"Being a democracy does not mean India has to have open borders." This piece in Organiser explains that foreign nationals hold no inalienable right to enter India. It says: "A visa is an administrative permission, which the competent authority may cancel in accordance with the law.  On the one hand, there is freedom of the press and of expression, which is a fundamental right of Indian citizens under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. On the other, there is the regulation of a foreign national’s entry into and departure from India, which falls entirely under immigration law and the discretionary power of the executive. The issuing of a visa does not create a permanent or irrevocable right of entry.  The right to reside and settle in India under Article 19 belongs only to Indian citizens. Foreign nationals cannot invoke Article 19(1)(a) or other freedoms to claim entry into, or permanent residence in, India. Press freedom does not create a right to enter another country, and that democratic openness does not require a nation to relinquish control of its borders. The cancellation of Helle Lyng’s visa is not an attack on press freedom. It is an exercise of the sovereign power of the Indian State, supported by the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025."

Text of My Keynote Address
Delivered at the National Press Day, 2026 celebrations organised by the National Union of Journalists (India), Hyderabad, on 16 November 2026.

*****

Distinguished office-bearers of the National Union of Journalists (India), members of the journalist fraternity, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen.

My greetings to all of you on #NationalPressDay2026.

I am delighted to address an issue that goes beyond the interests of journalists and media organisations. It concerns the survival of truth, the accountability of power and the foundations of democracy.

Artificial Intelligence is transforming how information is created and disseminated—and how people perceive reality. It offers extraordinary possibilities but also unprecedented dangers. In an age when reality itself can be manufactured, who will defend the truth?

For journalism, this is not merely a technological challenge. It is a test of credibility, independence and courage.

I would like to examine this challenge from a democratic and constitutional perspective.

1. AI AND THE MANUFACTURE OF REALITY

Every major technological revolution has transformed communication. The printing press expanded the dissemination of knowledge; radio and television transformed mass communication; the internet removed geographical barriers. Artificial Intelligence takes this transformation to an entirely different level.

Today, videos, voices, photographs, documents and entire narratives can be fabricated and presented as authentic. The consequences can be devastating: elections manipulated, reputations destroyed, social unrest provoked, national security threatened and the administration of justice compromised.

Yet AI can also assist journalism by analysing vast volumes of information, identifying patterns, translating Indian languages and helping uncover facts.
But one distinction is fundamental: the ability to manufacture information is not the ability to establish truth.

A convincing video is not necessarily genuine evidence. An algorithmically identified pattern is not proof of wrongdoing. A machine can generate a narrative, but it cannot assume responsibility for its veracity.

Verification, corroboration and independent human judgment remain indispensable.

AI may transform the tools of journalism. It must never be allowed to manufacture the truth that journalism is duty-bound to discover.

2. THE PRESS AND DEMOCRACY

A functioning democracy rests on four great institutions: the Legislature, the Executive, the Judiciary and the Free Press. The first three are constitutional organs of the State. The Press has evolved as the Fourth Estate, performing an equally indispensable democratic function.

Our National Emblem offers an interesting metaphor. The Lion Capital of Ashoka depicts four lions standing back to back. Three are visible; the fourth remains invisible. One could metaphorically associate that invisible fourth lion with the Press—not as a constitutional interpretation, but as a reminder of its indispensable democratic role.

The Legislature makes laws, the Executive implements them and the Judiciary interprets them and safeguards the rule of law. The Press informs citizens, scrutinises power, exposes wrongdoing and gives voice to public concerns.

It is the bridge between governance and the people, telling citizens what is done in their name, with their mandate and, most importantly, with their money.

Article 19(1)(a) of our Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression. The Supreme Court has recognised freedom of the Press as integral to this right, subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

Press freedom is not merely a professional privilege. It is also the citizen's right to receive information and form independent opinions.

The Press is not merely an observer of democracy. It enables citizens to question power and hold those who govern them accountable.

3. MEDIA INDEPENDENCE: FROM WHOM AND WHAT?

We frequently discuss press freedom in terms of censorship, governmental interference and intimidation. But the question of independence goes much deeper.

Independence from whom? Independence from what?

Is the Press independent of governments, political parties, corporate owners, commercial interests, ideological and religious influences? Is it independent of its own prejudices?

A Press free from governmental censorship but controlled by political patrons, corporate owners or ideological loyalties is not truly independent.

First: Independence from political ownership and control.

Political parties, politicians and their associates own, control or influence media organisations. At the same time, business interests increasingly enter politics, while politicians acquire commercial interests.
When business becomes politics and politics becomes business, the media becomes an instrument through which both protect their power and interests.

The expression Godi Media has become a widely used pejorative description of sections of the Indian mainstream media since 2014. It reflects the criticism that sections of the media have been manipulated, subdued or co-opted into functioning as publicity and propaganda instruments for the RSS-BJP political establishment and Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

The problem is not merely favourable coverage. It is the abandonment of scrutiny: governments are praised, opponents vilified and inconvenient questions suppressed.

As the saying goes, “A dog with a bone in its mouth cannot bark.”

Second: Independence from corporate and commercial interests.

Concentration of media ownership, dependence on advertising and commercial pressures can determine editorial priorities. The same business interests may have stakes in media, access to public finance and influence over political decisions.

Between FY2015 and FY2024, scheduled commercial banks wrote off approximately ₹16.35 lakh crore in bad loans, of which around ₹10 lakh crore was linked to big business houses.

Yet, where is the sustained media scrutiny? Where are the investigations into the beneficiaries and the accountability of those responsible?

When the powerful can influence both the flow of public money and the flow of public information, accountability itself is compromised.

Third: Independence of Journalists from Financial Vulnerability.

Journalists must receive fair and assured remuneration and reasonable employment security. Inadequate wages and precarious employment expose them to inducements and pressures that compromise their professional independence. Fair remuneration and employment security are therefore essential safeguards of independent journalism.

Fair remuneration is not merely an employment obligation; it is an essential safeguard of independent journalism.

Fourth: Independence from ideological and religious influence.

Journalists are entitled to personal political, ideological and religious convictions. But personal beliefs must never become professional prejudices. Ideology must not determine which facts are reported, which victims deserve sympathy or which perpetrators are spared scrutiny.

A journalist who applies different standards according to political allegiance or religious identity is practising partisanship, not independent journalism.

The most dangerous form of media control is not always censorship of what is published. It is control over what is never allowed to become a subject of public scrutiny.

Press independence must therefore be both institutional and intellectual: freedom from external control and freedom from prejudices that compromise professional judgment.

4. SELECTIVE JOURNALISM

Media capture by political, corporate and ideological interests has a direct consequence: selective journalism. Some events are amplified, others buried; some victims command national outrage, while others disappear from public consciousness.
Let me cite five examples.

First: Naxalism and Maoist insurgency.

For decades, sections of the intellectual and media establishment romanticised Naxalite and Maoist insurgents as revolutionaries and champions of the oppressed.

Marginalised populations have suffered genuine injustice, exploitation and deprivation. Their grievances deserve redressal. But reporting those grievances is fundamentally different from romanticising armed groups that exploit them to advance a violent, anti-democratic ideology.

Did the media adequately expose how deprivation and alienation were exploited to recruit cadres and perpetuate violence?

When journalism romanticises violent ideologies and neglects their victims, it risks becoming a propaganda instrument and force-multiplier for the very forces it ought to expose.

Second: The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus.

The genocide and religious cleansing of Kashmiri Hindus from their ancestral homeland remain one of the darkest and most shameful chapters in democratic India's history. Hindus were subjected to targeted killings, terror, threats and religious persecution. An entire Hindu community was driven out of Kashmir, and the Indian State was complicit.

And what did the Indian media do? Where was its outrage? Where were its investigations and sustained campaigns for justice and the safe return of the displaced?

The media's failure was not simply inadequate coverage. It was a complicit silence in the face of the genocide and religious cleansing of an entire community.

By its silence, the media helped erase the suffering of Kashmiri Hindus from the national conscience. That is an indictment of the media as much as it is of the State.

Third: The religious persecution of Hindus in the Northeast.

In the Christian-majority states of Mizoram and Meghalaya, Hindus have been facing severe religious persecution and discrimination. In some instances, they have been denied even the basic right to perform the last rites of their dead, to cremate their own family members in accordance with their religious traditions.

What could be more fundamental than this right? And where is the national media? Where are the headlines, investigations and expressions of outrage?

When the media turns a blind eye to the persecution of a community, it abandons the victims and shields the perpetrators from scrutiny.

Fourth: Double standards in reporting religiously sensitive crimes.

There is a glaring asymmetry in crime reporting. When the victim is Christian or Muslim, or the accused is Hindu, religious identity is often prominently highlighted. But when Hindus are victims, or the accused is Christian or Muslim, that identity disappears into generic descriptions or silence.

Why should the same journalistic standards not apply to everyone?

I demand equal seriousness of investigation, prominence of coverage and accountability, irrespective of the community involved.

The test of secular journalism is not whether it ignores religion, but whether it applies the same standards of fairness and scrutiny to everyone.

Fifth: Neutrality Must Not Become Complicity.

The media cannot be neutral between the perpetrator and the victim. Silence in the face of oppression emboldens the perpetrator and abandons the victim. Neutrality that fails to distinguish between the two is not impartiality; it is complicity.

Journalistic independence demands an unwavering commitment to truth and equal scrutiny of every government, political party, ideology and institution, irrespective of whose interests are affected.

5. FREEDOM AFTER SPEECH

A remark attributed to Idi Amin, the former President of Uganda, captures a fundamental danger: “There is freedom of speech, but I cannot guarantee freedom after speech.”

It exposes the hollowness of a freedom that exists only so long as it does not inconvenience those in power.

This brings me to an important constitutional proposition.

Article 19(1)(a), while guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression, is not adequate by itself to provide the explicit institutional recognition and safeguards that an independent Press requires. The Constitution must recognise the Free Press as an independent Fourth Estate of our democracy.

As National President of the Sarvjan Sanatan Party @sarvjansp, I affirm our commitment to pursuing a constitutional amendment to provide explicit constitutional recognition and status to the Press, so that not only freedom of speech but, importantly, freedom after speech is constitutionally guaranteed and enforced.

If the Press is indispensable to democracy, why should its institutional independence and constitutional status remain without explicit constitutional recognition?

I leave this question before this distinguished gathering.

Thank you.

Privacy vs Press Freedom: Where Should the Line Be Drawn?

Introduction

🌟 The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023, has reignited the constitutional debate between individual privacy and freedom of the press. The challenge is to protect personal dignity without undermining investigative journalism and the public's right to know.

Main Body

🌟 Constitutional Balance: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of expression, while Article 21 protects the right to privacy, recognised in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

🌟 Journalistic Independence: Mandatory consent for personal information could restrict investigative reporting and discourage whistleblowers from exposing wrongdoing.

🌟 Public Interest Test: In R. Rajagopal v. State of Tamil Nadu (1994), the Supreme Court distinguished legitimate public reporting from unjustified intrusion into private life.

🌟 Sting Operations: R.K. Anand v. Registrar, Delhi High Court (2009) recognised their public value in exposing misconduct, while Rajat Prasad v. CBI (2014) cautioned against treating sting operations as immunity from criminal liability.

🌟 Media Accountability: Sahara v. SEBI (2012) recognised temporary postponement of publication where publicity threatens a fair trial.

🌟 International Practice: The US, UK, Brazil and Kenya provide different forms of journalistic exemptions within data-protection frameworks.

Challenges

🌟 Balancing privacy with transparency and accountability.

🌟 Protecting confidential sources and whistleblowers.

🌟 Preventing trial by media and reputational damage.

🌟 Avoiding misuse of privacy laws to suppress scrutiny.

Constructive Criticism

🌟 Excessive consent requirements may create indirect censorship.

🌟 Unclear exemptions can generate regulatory uncertainty.

🌟 Investigative journalism may become vulnerable to legal intimidation.

🌟 Unrestricted reporting can violate individual dignity and fair-trial rights.

Way Forward

🌟 Introduce a clearly defined public-interest exemption.

🌟 Establish independent and proportionate oversight.

🌟 Protect confidential journalistic sources.

🌟 Develop safeguards against trial by media.

🌟 Harmonise data protection with constitutional freedoms.

Highlighted Keywords

🌟 Constitutional Balancing: Reconciling competing fundamental rights without allowing either to become absolute.

🌟 Public Interest: Information necessary for democratic accountability, not merely public curiosity.

🌟 Prior Restraint: Government-imposed restriction on publication before it occurs.

🌟 Trial by Media: Media coverage that prejudges guilt before judicial determination.

🌟 Proportionality: Restricting a right only to the extent necessary for a legitimate objective.

Conclusion

🌟 A mature democracy must protect both the individual's right to dignity and the press's duty to question power. Privacy must not become a shield for misconduct, nor press freedom a licence for intrusion.
